q: Going from equity value to enterprise value, which balance sheet item is subtracted?
explain: EV = equity value + debt + preferred stock + noncontrolling interest - cash and equivalents. Cash is subtracted because, in theory, an acquirer can use the target's cash to pay down part of the assumed debt.
hook: Add the claims, subtract the cash.

sources.title: Enterprise Value (EV) - Formula, Definition and Examples of EV
sources.quote: EV = Common Shares + Preferred Shares + Market Value of Debt + Noncontrolling Interest – Cash and Equivalents

sources.title: Enterprise Value (TEV) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: The rationale behind incorporating net debt rather than gross debt is that the cash sitting on a company’s balance sheet could hypothetically be used to pay down outstanding debt if deemed necessary.

q: Going from equity value to enterprise value, is preferred stock added or subtracted?
explain: Preferred stock is a non-common claim that is treated more like debt: it pays a fixed dividend, ranks ahead of common stock, and normally must be repaid in an acquisition.
hook: Preferred behaves like debt, so it goes on the same side as debt.

sources.title: Equity Value to Enterprise Value Bridge | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: From there, the company's net debt (i.e. total debt less cash ), preferred stock , and non-controlling interest (i.e. minority interest ) are added to the equity value.

sources.title: Enterprise Value (EV) - Formula, Definition and Examples of EV
sources.quote: They are treated more as debt, in this case, because they pay a fixed amount of dividends and have a higher priority in asset and earning claims than common stock. In an acquisition, they normally must be repaid just like debt.

q: Going from equity value to enterprise value, is noncontrolling (minority) interest added or subtracted?
explain: Noncontrolling interest is added because the parent consolidates all of the subsidiary's results, so EV must include the funding for the minority stake it does not own.
hook: Consolidated in the numbers, so consolidated in the value.

sources.title: Enterprise Value (TEV) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Enterprise Value (TEV) = Equity Value + Net Debt + Preferred Stock + Minority Interest

sources.title: What is Enterprise Value? - Training The Street
sources.quote: However, when we calculate EV, we need to include 100% of all the operating assets that the company consolidates – we therefore need to include the funding for the minority stake in the consolidated, but non-wholly owned assets (i.e. the NCI).

q: What percentage of a consolidated subsidiary's revenues, expenses and cash flow does the parent include in its own numbers, which is why NCI is added to EV?
explain: Under consolidation the parent reports 100% of the subsidiary's results even though it owns less than 100%, so NCI is added to keep EV consistent with consolidated metrics like EBITDA.
hook: Own 70%, report 100%: NCI fills the 30% gap.

sources.title: Enterprise Value (EV) - Formula, Definition and Examples of EV
sources.quote: We add this noncontrolling interest to the calculation of EV because the parent company has consolidated financial statements with that noncontrolling interest; meaning the parent includes 100% of the revenues, expenses, and cash flow in its numbers even though it doesn’t own 100% of the business.

sources.title: What is Enterprise Value? - Training The Street
sources.quote: However, when we calculate EV, we need to include 100% of all the operating assets that the company consolidates – we therefore need to include the funding for the minority stake in the consolidated, but non-wholly owned assets (i.e. the NCI).

q: A noncontrolling interest arises when a parent owns more than what percentage of a subsidiary, but less than 100%?
explain: Noncontrolling interest is the portion of a subsidiary not owned by a parent that holds a greater than 50% but less than 100% stake and consolidates the subsidiary.

sources.title: Enterprise Value (EV) - Formula, Definition and Examples of EV
sources.quote: Noncontrolling interest is the portion of a subsidiary not owned by the parent company (who owns a greater than 50% but less than 100% position in the subsidiary).

sources.title: What is Enterprise Value? - Training The Street
sources.quote: If a parent company owns between 50+% to 80% of a subsidiary, it will likely use the consolidation method to report the results of that entity

q: If a company raises new debt and keeps the proceeds as cash, what happens to its enterprise value?
explain: The new debt raises total debt, but the proceeds raise cash by the same amount, so net debt and therefore EV are unchanged.
hook: Debt up, cash up: net debt flat.

sources.title: Equity Value to Enterprise Value Bridge | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: However, a critical concept to understand is that the addition of new debt does NOT increase a company's enterprise value. The reason is newly raised capital via debt financing flows directly into the cash balance of the company, so the two offset each other, since net debt is the difference between total debt and cash.

q: Diluted equity value equals the share price multiplied by what?
explain: Equity value is calculated on a fully diluted basis, so potentially dilutive securities such as in-the-money options, warrants and convertibles are counted.

sources.title: Equity Value to Enterprise Value Bridge | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Equity Value = Latest Closing Share Price × Total Diluted Shares Outstanding

sources.title: Enterprise Value (EV) - Formula, Definition and Examples of EV
sources.quote: Equity value is found by taking the company’s fully-diluted shares outstanding and multiplying them by the stock’s current market price. Fully diluted means that it includes in-the-money options , warrants, and convertible securities, aside from just the basic shares outstanding.

q: Enterprise value is described as neutral to what, which makes it well suited to comparing companies with different financing?
explain: Because EV covers all capital providers, it is indifferent to how the business is financed, so EV multiples are independent of capital structure while equity multiples are affected by leverage.
hook: EV doesn't care how you pay for the business.

sources.title: Equity Value to Enterprise Value Bridge | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: The enterprise value metric is capital structure neutral and indifferent to discretionary financing decisions, making it well-suited for purposes of relative valuation and comparisons among different companies.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples - Financial Edge Training
sources.quote: This means that equity multiples are impacted by differing capital structures, whereas enterprise value multiples are independent of capital structure.

q: Under the standard convention, are equity method investments added to or subtracted from enterprise value?
explain: The parent records only its share of an equity method investee's profit below operating income, so the investee is not in consolidated EBITDA; subtracting the investment keeps EV/EBITDA consistent.
hook: Not in EBITDA, so take it out of EV.

sources.title: Enterprise Value Formula & Equation (2026) | CT Acquisitions
sources.quote: Yes, under the standard convention. The parent records only its share of an equity method investee’s profit below operating income, so none of that business is in consolidated EBITDA. Subtracting the investment keeps the EV/EBITDA multiple consistent: the numerator and the denominator then cover the same operating business.

sources.title: Equity Value - How to Calculate the Equity Value for a Firm
sources.quote: In most cases, both short-term and long-term investments are also subtracted; however, this requires an analyst’s judgment and depends on how liquid the securities are.

q: Under ASC 260's treasury stock method, exercise proceeds are assumed to repurchase common stock at what price?
accept: average market price during the period
explain: The treasury stock method assumes the proceeds from exercising options and warrants are used to buy back common stock at the average market price during the period.

sources.title: 4.2 Treasury Stock Method | DART – Deloitte Accounting Research Tool
sources.quote: The proceeds from exercise shall be assumed to be used to purchase common stock at the average market price during the period.

sources.title: 7.5 Diluted EPS (PwC Viewpoint)
sources.quote: Treasury stock method: A method of recognizing the use of proceeds that could be obtained upon exercise of options and warrants in computing diluted EPS. It assumes that any proceeds would be used to purchase common stock at the average market price during the period.

q: The treasury stock method is applied only to options and warrants that are what?
explain: Out-of-the-money options are excluded because a holder would not exercise them and including them would generally be antidilutive.

sources.title: 4.2 Treasury Stock Method | DART – Deloitte Accounting Research Tool
sources.quote: The treasury stock method is only applied to options and warrants that are in-the-money from the perspective of the counterparty.

sources.title: Treasury Stock Method - Definition, Formula, and Example
sources.quote: The treasury stock method is a way for companies to calculate how many additional shares may be generated from outstanding in-the-money warrants and options.

q: Which method is used to calculate the dilutive effect of stock options and warrants?
explain: Options and warrants use the treasury stock method, while convertible debt and convertible preferred stock use the if-converted method.

sources.title: Financial reporting insights: earnings per share (RSM, October 2024)
sources.quote: Warrants Treasury stock method

sources.title: ASC 260-10 Overall — ASC Reader
sources.quote: Diluted EPS uses the treasury stock method for options, warrants, and share-based awards

q: Which method is used to reflect convertible debt in diluted EPS?
explain: Convertible debt and convertible preferred stock use the if-converted method, which assumes conversion into common shares.

sources.title: Financial reporting insights: earnings per share (RSM, October 2024)
sources.quote: Convertible debt If-converted method

sources.title: If-Converted Method for Diluted EPS | Farhat Lectures
sources.quote: Convertible bonds and convertible preferred stock. Stock options and warrants use the treasury stock method instead.

q: Under the if-converted method, on what tax basis is a convertible bond's interest expense added back to the EPS numerator?
explain: If the bonds had converted, the company would save the interest but pay more income tax, so net income rises only by the after-tax interest.
hook: Interest is tax-deductible, so the add-back is after tax.

sources.title: Demystifying Convertible Bonds - April 2024 - Latham & Watkins
sources.quote: the after-tax effect of the interest expense for the notes during the reporting period is added back to the numerator of EPS

sources.title: If-Converted Method for Diluted EPS | Farhat Lectures
sources.quote: Interest expense reduces taxable income. If the bonds had been converted, the company would save the interest but pay more income tax, so net income rises only by the after-tax amount.

q: Under the if-converted method for convertible preferred stock, what is added back to the EPS numerator?
explain: The preferred dividends subtracted in basic EPS are added back in full, with no tax effect, and the shares issuable on conversion are added to the denominator.

sources.title: If-Converted Method for Diluted EPS | Farhat Lectures
sources.quote: Convertible preferred stock | Add back the preferred dividends subtracted in basic EPS (no tax effect) | Add the common shares issuable on conversion

sources.title: ASC 260-10 Overall — ASC Reader
sources.quote: the if-converted method for convertible securities (add back preferred dividends or after-tax interest and assume conversion at the beginning of the period)

q: A convertible bond's conversion price equals its principal amount divided by what?
explain: The conversion ratio is the number of shares received per bond (usually per $1,000 of principal); principal divided by that ratio gives the effective price paid per share.

sources.title: Financial Reporting Developments - Earnings per share (EY)
sources.quote: Conversion price = (Convertible bond’s principal amount) ÷ (Conversion ratio) = $1,000 ÷ 20 = $50.

sources.title: Convertible bonds: US GAAP and hidden financing costs
sources.quote: The conversion price is the principal divided by the conversion ratio, and is the effective price per share the holder pays by giving up the bond.

q: How many shares does $1,000 of convertible bond principal convert into at a $25 conversion price?
explain: Shares per bond equal principal divided by conversion price: $1,000 / $25 = 40 shares per $1,000 principal.

sources.title: Convertible Bonds - Mayer Brown (2025)
sources.quote: Initial Conversion Rate = $1,000 principal amount of notes divided by conversion price – = $1,000 divided by $25 per share = 40 shares per $1,000 principal amount of bonds

sources.title: Convertible bonds: US GAAP and hidden financing costs
sources.quote: The conversion ratio is the number of shares received on converting a bond, usually stated per $1,000 of principal. The conversion price is the principal divided by the conversion ratio

q: In the enterprise value bridge, how is an out-of-the-money convertible bond counted?
explain: When the share price is below the conversion price, the holder is unlikely to convert, so the face value is counted as debt and no shares are added.
hook: Out of the money: stays a bond.

sources.title: Equity Value and Enterprise Value Questions & Answers
sources.quote: If the Convertible Bonds are out-of-the-money, then you count the face value of the convertibles as part of the company’s Debt.

sources.title: Convertible Bonds Explained for IB Interviews
sources.quote: If the stock price is below the conversion price (out of the money), the convertible is treated as debt and added to enterprise value.

q: What error occurs if an in-the-money convertible is counted both as debt in the EV bridge and as diluted shares?
explain: An in-the-money convertible should be added as diluted shares and removed from debt; leaving it in both places counts the same claim twice and overstates EV.

sources.title: Convertible Securities and Warrants: Valuation and Dilution
sources.quote: The critical rule: never include a convertible in both the debt component of EV and the diluted share count simultaneously.

sources.title: Enterprise value vs equity value · Premieur Institute
sources.quote: If the shares are counted and the bond is also left in net debt, the same claim appears twice and EV is overstated by the face value of the bond.

q: Potential common shares whose inclusion would increase EPS are described as what, and are excluded from diluted EPS?
explain: ASC 260 does not assume conversion, exercise or contingent issuance of securities that would have an antidilutive effect on EPS.

sources.title: Handbook: Earnings per share - KPMG
sources.quote: Potential common shares are not included in diluted EPS if they are antidilutive – i.e. the exercise or conversion would increase EPS.

sources.title: 4.1 Background | DART – Deloitte Accounting Research Tool
sources.quote: 45-17 The computation of diluted EPS shall not assume conversion, exercise, or contingent issuance of securities that would have an antidilutive effect on EPS.

q: Under ASC 260's treasury stock method, options are assumed exercised at what point (unless issued later)?
explain: Exercise is assumed at the beginning of the period, or at the time of issuance if later, and the resulting incremental shares go into the diluted EPS denominator.

sources.title: 4.2 Treasury Stock Method | DART – Deloitte Accounting Research Tool
sources.quote: Exercise of options and warrants shall be assumed at the beginning of the period (or at time of issuance, if later) and common shares shall be assumed to be issued.

sources.title: Financial reporting insights: earnings per share (RSM, October 2024)
sources.quote: Assume the outstanding options and warrants are exercised at the beginning of the reporting period (or at time of issuance, if later) and common shares are issued at that time.

q: Under the treasury stock method, how many net new shares come from 15,000 in-the-money options with a $7 exercise price and a $10 average share price?
explain: Proceeds of 15,000 x $7 = $105,000 buy back $105,000 / $10 = 10,500 shares, so net new shares are 15,000 - 10,500 = 4,500.

sources.title: Treasury Stock Method - Definition, Formula, and Example
sources.quote: Using these proceeds, the company can buy $105,000 / $10 = 10,500 shares at the average market price. Thus, the net increase in shares outstanding is 15,000 – 10,500 = 4,500.

sources.title: Treasury Stock Method: Diluted EPS for Options and Warrants
sources.quote: When exercise cash is the only assumed proceeds, use this shortcut for dilutive options: incremental shares = number of options × (average market price − exercise price) ÷ average market price .

q: Because EBITDA is calculated before interest expense, it pairs with which value measure in a multiple?
explain: EBITDA does not deduct net interest expense and represents all investors, so it pairs with enterprise value; an Equity Value/EBITDA multiple is considered meaningless.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Full Tutorial, Excel, and Video
sources.quote: For example, EBITDA does not deduct a company’s Net Interest Expense, and it represents all the investors in the company. Therefore, it always pairs with Enterprise Value.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Enterprise vs Equity, P/E, EBITDA, EBIT, Sales | Macabacus
sources.quote: For example, when talking about the EV/EBITDA multiple, we would simply say “EBITDA multiple”, because the only sensible numerator is EV.

q: The P/E multiple is equivalent to equity value divided by what?
explain: P/E is share price over EPS; dividing both equity value and net income by fully diluted shares gives the same ratio.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Enterprise vs Equity, P/E, EBITDA, EBIT, Sales | Macabacus
sources.quote: Note that the P/E multiple equals the ratio of equity value to net Income, in which the numerator and denominator are both are divided by the number of fully diluted shares.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Full Tutorial, Excel, and Video
sources.quote: Equity Value / Net Income (P / E): Tells you how valuable a company is in relation to its after-tax profits

q: Is price-to-book (P/B) an enterprise value multiple or an equity value multiple?
explain: Book value represents only the common shareholders, so P/B is an equity value multiple, alongside P/E and the PEG ratio.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples Primer | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Enterprise Value Multiples | Equity Value Multiples * * EV/EBITDA | * P/E Ratio * * EV/EBIT | * PEG Ratio * * EV/Revenue | * Price/Book Ratio (P/B)

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Full Tutorial, Excel, and Video
sources.quote: OR does the metric represent just the common shareholders? If so, it pairs with Equity Value (e.g., Book Value ).

q: Denominators of enterprise value multiples must be computed before which expense that goes to lenders?
explain: EV multiples use metrics relevant to all stakeholders, so the denominator is before interest, preferred dividends and minority interest expense; a metric that deducts net interest pairs with equity value.
hook: Above the interest line = EV; below it = equity.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Enterprise vs Equity, P/E, EBITDA, EBIT, Sales | Macabacus
sources.quote: Therefore, the relevant denominator must be computed before interest expense, preferred dividends, and minority interest expense.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Full Tutorial, Excel, and Video
sources.quote: Does the metric deduct the company’s Net Interest Expense? If so, it pairs with Equity Value (e.g., Net Income ).

q: According to CFA Institute, EV/EBITDA is preferred to P/EBITDA because EBITDA is a flow to whom?
explain: EBITDA is a pre-interest number, so it belongs to all capital providers and matches EV; equity value only covers shareholders.

sources.title: Market-Based Valuation: Price and Enterprise Value Multiples | CFA Institute
sources.quote: EV/EBITDA is preferred to P/EBITDA because EBITDA, as a pre-interest number, is a flow to all providers of capital.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Enterprise vs Equity, P/E, EBITDA, EBIT, Sales | Macabacus
sources.quote: Similarly, an Equity Value/EBITDA multiple is meaningless because the numerator applies only to shareholders, while the denominator accrues to all holders of capital.

q: For comparing companies with different capital structures, which is conceptually preferable: P/S or EV/Sales?
explain: Sales is a pre-financing metric that belongs to all capital providers, so pairing it with EV makes companies with different leverage comparable.

sources.title: Market-Based Valuation: Price and Enterprise Value Multiples | CFA Institute
sources.quote: The ratio of EV to total sales is conceptually preferable to P/S because EV/S facilitates comparisons among companies with varying capital structures.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples - Financial Edge Training
sources.quote: This means that enterprise value and enterprise value multiples are independent of capital structure.

q: Why does the if-converted method have no share buyback offset, unlike the treasury stock method?
explain: Option exercise brings in cash that the treasury stock method assumes is used to repurchase shares; converting a bond brings in no cash, so all conversion shares are added.
hook: No cash in, nothing to buy back with.

sources.title: Convertible Securities and Warrants: Valuation and Dilution
sources.quote: If-converted method: Used for convertible bonds and convertible preferred stock. Assumes the convertible is converted into common shares. Since the company receives no cash upon conversion (unlike option exercise), there is no buyback offset.

sources.title: Equity Value and Enterprise Value Questions & Answers
sources.quote: Treatment is “either or” – they count as debt, or count 100% as additional shares, with no Treasury Stock Method involved
